chapter: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
title: High-note trumpeters: Jenkins, Stewart, Cat Anderson, Killian
summary: He recalls Freddie Jenkins as Little Posey, then Rex Stewart, Cat Anderson, and Al Killian.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Who was the first high note trumpet player in the band?
In the band?
Uh-huh.

Freddie Jenkins played the high notes. We used to call him Little Posey. He was on the end. He was a small fellow and very flashy, and it seems that every man that became a member of that band had some quality that attrac-

ted the public.
Now Little Posey was very flashy and was used so many, many times for his flashing. He just fit, everything just fit in like a puzzle in this odd picture, and now Little Posey -- who, incidentally, I hear is still alive -- has long been forgotten, seemingly. He's down in Texas. I hear he's a deputy sheriff in Fort Worth, or someplace down in there. And because of some physical ailments he's no longer able to play horn -- a horn, and all of these people all the way along fit into this picture, and all of them were instrumental and all of them were important in the part that they fit.
Freddie was called Posey because of what?

Well, he would pose, you know, everything with him was a picture, very pleasant-natured little fellow, and that's why they called him Little Posey. He was small and everything he did was posed, in a pose.
Who was the next high note player?

I would imagine Rex Stewart, when he joined the band he became executor of the high notes, and then, let's see, after Rex, "Cat" Anderson. Well "Cat" was the -- I think was the greatest of the high note men. In fact, he is still playing, and he's still hitting high notes as he did before.
I attended a showing of the Ice Follies out here in

Los Angeles, and I heard this trumpet way up in the air and I said that's got to be Cat Anderson, and sure enough, later on I found on that was Cat Anderson, still hitting them strong and terrifically high.
And he was in and out of Duke's band several times.
Yes, Yes. Originally I think Cat came with Lionel Hampton's band, into the east, then he came over to Ellington.
Didn't he have his own band recently?

He had his own band, yes. He had a little band and in and out. They all try to, you know, advance themselves by getting a band, but usually there's too much pressure, too much hard work, and they're not used to it, and they usually tire out quickly and go back to other bands.
After Cat left in the forties, Al Killian (inaudible), right?
No, I think -- no, that's right, Killian was first.
Wasn't Cat there before Al, and then after, again?
I'm not sure of that. But Killian was a high note man also.
Did he play as high as Cat?
No, not quite, nor as strong. No, Cat
was very strong.

I remember in the high note ending of one of the dances in the "Liberian Suite," when Killian would play those high notes, and Kay Davis would be standing in the wings singing the high notes right along with Killian's trumpet.
Uh-huh, yes. Killian was nice, very nice trumpet player. But we'd say that Cat was like a bull. He was very strong.
And Al was killed here in 1950, (inaudible).
Yeah, uh-huh.
And then there wasn't another really high note trumpet player until Cat went back into the band, was there?
No, I don't think so.
